In the French army sharp-shooter; a skirmisher; one of an ganized body of light troops for skirmish du {{smaller block|The title ''tirailleurs'' was first applied in 1792 to Fre light-armed troops who were thrown out from the m body to bring on an action, cover an attack, or gener to annoy or deceive the enemy.}} '''tirannye†''', '''tirandye†''', ''n.'' Obsolete forms ''tyranny''. '''tirant†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''tyrant''. '''tirasse''' (ti-ras′), ''n.'' [< F. ''tirasse'', a draw- a strap, < ''tirer'', draw: see ''tire''2.] In ''org building'', same as ''pedal coupler'' (which see, der ''pedal''). '''tiraunt†''', '''tirauntrie†'''. Old spellings of ''tyr'' ''tyrantry''. '''tiraz''', ''n.'' A costly silk stuff of which the m famous manufacture seems to have been at meria in Spain, under the Moorish dominati it is mentioned as woven with inscriptions, names of distinguished men, etc. '''tire'''1 (tīr), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''tired'', ppr. ''tir'' [Early mod. E. also ''tyre''; < ME. ''tiren'', ''tirien'', ''rien'', < AS. ''teorian'', intr. be tired, tr. tire, fatig cf. ME. ''a-teorien'', < AS. ''ā-teorian'', tire; appa secondary form of ''teran'', tear: see ''tear''1. verb has also been referred to ME. ''terien'', ''ter'' ''terwen'', ''terren'', ''tarien'', < AS. ''tergan'', vex (see ''t'' ''tarry''2), also to ''tire''2, pull, seize (see ''tire''2).] ''intrans.'' To become weary, fatigued, or jad have the strength or the patience reduced exhausted. {{smaller block|As true as truest horse that yet would never ''tire''. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 1}} I ''tired'' of the routine of eight years in one afternoon desired liberty. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyr}}}} {{smaller block|Nor mine the sweetness or the skill,
But mine the love that will not ''tire''. {{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make weary, weaken, or haust by exertion; fatigue; weary: used w reference to physical effect from either ph cal or mental strain. {{smaller block|''Tired'' limbs, and over-busy thoughts,
Inviting sleep and soft forgetfulness. {{right|''Wordsworth'', Excursion}}}} {{smaller block|Last year, Esther said innocently, she had no on help her, and the work ''tired'' her so. {{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p.}}}} {{smaller block|Music that gentlier on the spirit lies
Than ''tir'd'' eyelids upon ''tir'd'' eyes. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lotos-Eaters, Choric S}}}} '''2.''' To exhaust the attention or the patie of, as with dullness or tediousness; sati sicken, or cause repugnance in, as by excess supply or continuance; glut. {{smaller block|The feast, the dance; whate'er mankind desire,
E'en the sweet charms of sacred numbers ''tire''. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xiii.}}}} {{smaller block|Dramatic performances ''tired'' him [William of Oran {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng.,}}}} {{smaller block|I often grew
''Tired'' of so much within our little life. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lucre}}}} '''To tire out''', {{smaller|to weary or fatigue to the point of exh tion.}} {{smaller block|And some with Patents, some with Merit, ''Tir'd out'' my good Lord Dorset's Spirit. {{right|''Prior'', To Fleetwood Shepherd (1}}}} {{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Tire, Fatigue, Weary, Jade.'' These words are marily physical, and are in the order of strength. may become ''tired'' simply by standing still, or ''fatigue'' a little over-exertion. ''Fatigue'' suggests something o haustion or inability to continue exertion: as, ''fati'' with running. ''Weary'' implies protracted exertio strain gradually wearing out one's strength. ''Jade'' im the repetition of the same sort of exertion: as, a h will become ''jaded'' sooner by driving on a dead level if he occasionally has a hill to climb. All these w have a figurative application to the mind correspon to their physical meaning. See ''fatigue'', ''n.'', and ''wearis''}} '''tire'''1 (tīr), ''n.'' [< ''tire''1, ''v.''] The feeling of be tired; a sensation of physical or mental tigue. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|I have had a little cold for several days, and that the ''tire'' in me gives me some headache to-day. {{right|''S. Bowles'', in Merriam, I.}}}} {{smaller|'''Brain-tire.''' Same as ''brain-fag''.}} '''tire'''2† (tīr), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. ''tyre''; < ME. ''ti'' ''tyren'' (= Dan. ''tirre'', tease, worry), < OF. ( F.) ''tirer'' = Sp. Pg. ''tirar'' = It. ''tirare'', < ML ''rare'', draw, drag, pull, extend, produce, tract, prolong, etc.; prob. of Teut. origi Goth. ''tairan'' = AS. ''teran'', etc., tear: see ''te'' with which ''tire''2 seems to have been in part fused in ME. Cf. ''tire''1, prob. from the same root.] I. ''trans.'' 1. To draw; pull; drag. {{smaller block|Blauncheflur bid forth hire suere [neck], And Floriz aȝen hire gan ''tire''. {{right|''King Horn'' (E. E. T. S.), p}}}} 2. To pull apart or to pieces; rend and devo prey upon. {{smaller block|Thow endurest wo
As sharpe as doth he Sysiphus in helle,
Whose stomak fowles ''tyren'' everemo. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 787.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To engage in pulling or tearing or rending; raven; prey: used especially in falconry of hawks pouncing upon their prey, and in analogous figurative applications. {{smaller block|Upon whose breast a fiercer gripe doth ''tire''
Than did on him who first stole down the fire. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'' (Arber's Eng. Garner, I. 510).}} And, like an empty eagle,
''Tire'' on the flesh of me and of my son. {{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., i. 1. 268.}} Thus made she her remove,
And left wrath ''tyring'' on her son, for his enforced love. {{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, i. 422.}} Rivet him
To Caucasus, should he but frown; and let
His own gaunt eagle fly at him, to ''tire''. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iii. 1.}}}} Hence—'''2.''' To be earnestly engaged; dwell; dote; gloat. {{smaller block|I grieve myself
To think, when thou shalt be disedged by her
That now thou ''tirest'' on, how thy memory
Will then be pang'd by me. {{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, iii. 4. 96.}}}} '''tire'''3† (tīr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''tyre''; < OF. (and F.) ''tire'', a draught, pull, stretch, fling, length of course, etc. (in a great variety of senses) (= Sp. Pg. ''tiro'', a draught, shot, cast, throw, = It. ''tiro'', a draught, shot, etc.), < ''tirer'', draw: see ''tire''2, ''v.'' The form ''tier'', once a mere var. spelling of ''tire'' (like ''fier'' for ''fire''), is now pronounced differently, and, with ''tire'', is by some referred to a different source: see ''tier''2.] '''1.''' A train or series. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Such one was Wrath, the last of this ungodly ''tire'' [of passions]. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. iv. 35.}}}} '''2.''' A row; rank; course; tier; especially, a row of guns; a battery. {{smaller block|Hauing spent before in fight the one side of her ''tire'' of Ordinance, . . . she prepared to cast about, and to bestow on him the other side. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', I. 609.}} In view
Stood rank'd of seraphim another row,
In posture to displode their second ''tire''
Of thunder. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 605.}}}} '''3.''' A stroke; hit. ''Cotgrave.'' '''tire'''4 (tīr), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''tired'', ppr. ''tiring''. [Early mod. E. also ''tyre''; < ME. ''tiren'', ''tyren''; by apheresis from ''attire'', ''v.''] '''1.''' To adorn; attire; dress. See ''attire''. {{smaller block|Goth yond to a gret lord that gayly is ''tyred''. {{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 263.}} She painted her face, and ''tired'' her head. {{right|2 Ki. ix. 30.}} She speaks as she goes ''tired'' in cobweb-lawn, light, thin. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of His Humour, ii. 1.}}}} '''2.''' To prepare or equip for; make ready; set up. {{smaller block|But built anew with strength-conferring fare,
With limbs and soul untam'd, he ''tires'' a war. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xix. 168.}}}} '''tire'''4 (tīr), ''n.'' [By apheresis from ''attire'', ''n.''] '''1.''' Attire; dress. {{smaller block|He tore Dame Maudlin's silken ''tire''. {{right|''Scott.''}}}} '''2†.''' Furniture; apparatus; machinery. {{smaller block|Immediate sieges, and the ''tire'' of war, Roll in thy eager mind. {{right|''J. Philips'', Blenheim.}}}} '''tire5''' (tīr), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''tyre''; perhaps a modified form of ''tiar'', to simulate ''tire''4; otherwise simply a particular use of ''tire''4.] A head-dress. See ''tiara''. {{smaller block|On her head she wore a ''tyre'' of gold. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. x. 31.}} The best dresser of ''tires'' that ever busked the tresses of a Queen. {{right|''Scott'', Abbot, xxxi.}}}} '''tire6†''', ''n.'' [Also, erroneously, ''tier''; < ME. ''tyre'', prob. < OF. ''tire'', a draught, and thus ult. identical with ''tire''3.] A bitter drink or liquor. ''Halliwell.'' {{smaller block|W. Y. Index and hise wyf were here with here meny and here hors in our ladyes place, &c., on Saterday at evyn, and yedyn hens on Monday after none, whan summe had drunkyn malvyseye and ''tyre'', &c. {{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 511.}}}} '''tire7''' (tīr), ''n.'' [Prop. ''tier''; < ''tie''1 + ''-er''1.] A continuous band of metal or other substance placed around a wheel to form the tread. {{smaller|The tire may serve to resist shock, or hold the wheel together, or reduce wear, etc. Metal tires were formerly made in sections and bolted to the wheel, but in modern practice the tire is always a continuous band, expanded by heat and shrunk on over the wheel, at once to compress it and to secure a firm hold. Tires of rubber are used for bicycles, and are protected by thin plates of iron, and similar tires are used for wheels of traction-engines, etc. Also ''tyre''.}}—'''Tire-upsetting machine''', {{smaller|a machine for shrinking tires without cutting. The tire is heated, and then seized by movable clamps and strongly compressed to thicken it in one part and thus make it shorter, and while still hot it is placed on the wheel and permitted to shrink in place. ''E. H. Knight.''}} '''tire7''' (tīr), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''tired'', ppr. ''tiring''. [< ''tire''7, ''n.''] To put a tire upon; furnish with tires: as, to ''tire'' a wheel or a wagon. Also ''tyre''. {{smaller block|The tread may be turned down like the tread of a steel-''tired'' wheel, and will not glaze over and become smooth like iron. {{right|''Elect. Rev.'' (Amer.), XVI. x. 2.}}}} '''tire8''', ''n.'' See ''tier''1, 2. '''tire-bender''' (tīr′ben″dėr), ''n.'' A machine for bending the tires of wheels to the curve required by the rim of the wheel. {{smaller|Two forms are used: in one, three rollers are employed, between which the tire is passed, to cause it to bend to a circular shape; in the other form, the tire is drawn and bent round a cylinder of the size of the wheel.}} '''tire-bolt''' (tīr′bōlt), ''n.'' A screw-bolt by which a tire is fastened upon a wheel-center. {{smaller|If the wheel is made with retaining rings, the bolts are passed through these, and thus secure at once rings, center, and tire. See cut under ''bolt''.}} '''tiredness''' (tīrd′nes), ''n.'' The state of being tired; weariness; exhaustion. {{smaller block|It is not through the ''tirednesse'' or age of the earth, . . . but through our owne negligence, that it hath not satisfied vs so bountifully as it hath done. {{right|''Hakewill'', Apology, p. 143.}}}} '''tire-drill''' (tīr′dril), ''n.'' A machine for boring the holes for the bolts in tires. {{smaller|It has an adjustable clamp to hold the tire opposite the drill, which is advanced by a screw and crank.}} '''tire-heater''' (tīr′hē″tėr), ''n.'' A form of furnace for heating a tire to cause it to expand, in order that it may be fitted over the rim of a wheel. '''tireless1''' (tīr′les), ''a.'' [< ''tire''1, ''v.'', + ''-less''.] Not tiring or becoming tired; not yielding to fatigue; untiring; unwearying. {{smaller|[A word analogous in formation to ''ceaseless, exhaustless, relentless,'' etc., and long in every-day use, though omitted from dictionaries.]}} {{smaller block|He [the gaucho] was courageous and cruel, active and ''tireless'', never more at ease than when on the wildest horse. {{right|''Harper's Mag.'', LXXXII. 866.}}}} '''tireless2''' (tīr′les), ''a.'' [< ''tire''7 + ''-less''.] Without a tire: as, a ''tireless'' wheel. '''tirelessly''' (tīr′les-li), ''adv.'' In a tireless manner; without becoming tired; unweariedly. {{smaller block|She [Queen Victoria] does not go to the theatre, leaving that branch of the public duty of a sovereign to the Prince of Wales, who ''tirelessly'' pursues it. {{right|''New York Tribune'', March 22, 1891.}}}} '''tirelessness''' (tīr′les-nes), ''n.'' The property or character of being tireless; indefatigability. '''tireling†''' (tīr′ling), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''tyreling''; < ''tire''1 + ''-ling''1.] Tired; fatigued; fagged. {{smaller block|His ''tyreling'' Jade he fiersly forth did push Through thicke and thin, both over banck and bush. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. i. 17.}}}} '''tirelire''' (tēr′lēr), ''n.'' [< F. ''tirelire'', a money-box, formerly also a Christmas box (also the warbling of a lark: see ''tirra-lirra'').] A saving-box, popularly called “savings-bank,” usually made of baked clay, and of simple form, which must be broken in order to get at the money. '''tireman''' (tīr′man), ''n.''; pl. ''tiremen'' (-men). [< ''tire''4 + ''man''.] 1. A man who attends to the attiring of another; a dresser, especially in a theater; a valet. [Obsolete or rare.] {{smaller block|Enter the ''Tiremen'' to mend the lights. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Staple of News, Ind.}}}} 2. A dealer in clothes and articles of dress. ''Halliwell.'' '''tire-measurer''' (tīr′mezh″ṳ̄r-ėr), ''n.'' An instrument for measuring the circumference of a wheel or a tire. {{smaller|It consists essentially of a graduated wheel turning in a frame held by a handle, and in use is caused to run over the circumference of the wheel or tire to be measured.}} '''tirement†''' (tīr′ment), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. ''tyrement''; < ''tire''4 + ''-ment''.] An article of apparel; attire. {{smaller block|Owre women in playes and tryumphes haue not greater plentie of stones of glasse and crystall in theyr garlandes, crownes, gerdels, and suche other ''tyrementes''. {{right|''Peter Martyr'' (tr. in Eden's First Books on America, ed. [Arber, p. 89).}}}} '''tire-press''' (tīr′pres), ''n.'' A powerful hydraulic press for forcing the tires upon or removing them from the rims of locomotive driving-wheels. '''tire-roller''' (tīr′rō″lėr), ''n.'' A rolling-mill for wheel-tires. {{smaller|The rolls overhang their bearings, and can be moved to or from each other to admit the tire between}} them. ''E. H. Knight.'' '''tire-setter''' (tīr′set″ėr), ''n.'' A machine for setting a tire upon a wagon- or carriage-wheel. {{smaller|The tire is placed loose upon the wheel, and the machine, by the aid of thin steel bands which are drawn tight by means of a screw, upsets the tire, and presses it upon the wheel.}} '''tire-shrinker''' (tīr′shring″kėr), ''n.'' A machine for shortening a tire when, by shrinkage of the wheel, it has become loose. {{smaller|The tire is heated, and placed in the machine, which compresses the heated part, and thus reduces the diameter of the tire.}} '''tiresmith''' (tīr′smith), ''n.'' One who makes tires and other ironwork for coaches, etc. ''Imp. Dict.''
